transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-04-02 16:00 UTC, Duration ~48m
Attendees: Avery Mitchell (Redwood AE), Ravi Desai (Redwood SE), Sofia Alvarez (Redwood SE), Leah Kim (CTO, SparrowEdge), Ben Foster (SRE), Maya Ortiz (Product), Arjun Patel (Infra)

Summary: Quick discovery on multi-region failover, streaming latency p95 targets, and burst token/sec readiness. Customer runs a mixed synchronous streaming chat + async summarization workload. Main concerns: p95 under traffic spikes, failover consistency across regions, cost tradeoffs for Dedicated vs Hosted.

[00:00] Avery: hey everyone, thanks for carving time today; quick intros and then we'll jump into your workload and targets, uh, Leah do you want to start?
[00:18] Leah: sure yeah, I'm Leah, CTO. At a high level SparrowEdge runs a real-time agent for customer support and a nightly batch summarizer. The real-time path requires streaming token by token responses to customers; we target p95 latency under 300ms for the first token, and steady-state ~50ms per subsequent token ideally.
[00:40] Ben: hi, Ben SRE, we also need to support sudden bursts — Black Friday-like patterns — we saw 4x baseline for 10 minutes last year, so concurrency can spike from 200 to ~800 streams.
[00:58] Maya: product — we're trialing multimodal prompts next quarter; want to understand whether Redwood Hosted with routing to Dedicated can meet SLOs and also how Private would change the picture.
[01:15] Ravi: great, thanks. couple clarifying q's — when you say first-token p95 300ms is that inclusive of network egress to end-user? or just model-side generation?
[01:28] Leah: that's end-to-end to the browser. Our infra sits in us-west and eu-west; we prefer multi-region failover to avoid cross-continental hops.
[01:38] Sofia: okay. Are you currently doing any KV or prefix caching for repeated prompts? you mentioned some templates.
[01:45] Ben: yes, we have a small cache for system prompts and persona context. But most requests are fairly unique; caching helps maybe 10 to 15% of tokens.
[01:54] [02:00] Avery: helpful. can you share typical sequence length and token/sec per stream?
[02:06] Maya: average 120 tokens per response, bursty tokens/sec early in session when multiple messages are interleaved — we measured ~18 tokens/sec per stream at peak.
[02:16] Ravi: ok so mathematically, 800 concurrent streams * 18 tokens/sec -> 14.4k tokens/sec peak. For a hosted single region that translates to X GPU footprint depending on model; we usually map that to batch sizing and decoding footprint. (brief noise)
[02:35] Leah: also want to understand fallbacks — if the main model is quantized or a faster variant, do we lose quality in ways that break downstream routing?
[02:45] Ravi: yes so there are two levers — model variant fallback and routing to a different capacity tier. Redwood supports automatic fallback policies: you can prefer hosted low-latency model, then fallback to a quantized variant or Dedicated if latency rises. Fallbacks are configurable per route.
[03:05] Ben: how do you preserve conversation KV cache across region failover? if a request goes to us-west and then fails over to eu-west, the conversation history needs to be available.
[03:16] Sofia: good question. we recommend using a synchronized prefix store or attach the KV blob in the request; for strict consistency across regions we can run a shared KV in the control plane (private deployments) or replicate via your DB with a TTL. There are tradeoffs on latency.
[03:35] [03:50] Leah: latency cost tradeoffs — if we go Dedicated, do we get guaranteed p95 from Redwood or is that still probabilistic?
[03:57] Avery: Dedicated gives stronger guarantees and predictable throughput, we provide SLA targets for uptime and baseline latency tiers; exact p95 depends on model and packing, but we will size the Dedicated pool to meet your SLO for normal operation and define fallbacks for headroom.
[04:12] Ravi: to be concrete, for similar customers we sized a Dedicated of 4x A100-class units to sustain ~15k tokens/sec with streaming and p95 first token ~250–300ms region-local. Those are reference numbers; we'll run a tailored benchmark.
[04:29] Ben: when you say 15k tokens/sec is that with batching enabled? and what's the impact on first-token latency?
[04:37] Ravi: yes batching helps throughput; Redwood continuous batching tries to keep first-token latency low by micro-batching and prewarmed KV cache. There's a small tradeoff: heavy batching improves tokens/sec but can increase first-token p95 by 10–30ms depending on queueing.
[04:55] [05:10] Maya: and for streaming — do you stream partial tokens or do you buffer micro-chunks?
[05:15] Sofia: we stream at subtoken boundaries where possible, but it also depends on model tokenizer behavior. For many models we can flush partial tokens early to hit perceived low-latency in the UI. Some customers call that perceived latency optimization.
[05:30] Leah: security question — if we use Hosted but want single-tenant encryption, how does KMS and audit logs look?
[05:38] Avery: Hosted supports customer-managed keys via KMS and we provide audit logs for all requests; if you need VPC/private control plane we'd move to Private where logs and keys are under your control. We'll share the security pack.
[05:52] [06:10] Ben: one of our constraints is cold-starts when a model is pulled into a region; how long to warm up and can Redwood keep warm spares?
[06:18] Ravi: model load time varies by size; for large models it's minutes. We support warm pools and pre-allocate instances in Dedicated and Private. In Hosted we provide burst capacity but you should expect some ramp; we can configure warm standby for enterprise.
[06:35] Leah: ok, let's talk numbers for a POC. we want to run a 24-hour stress window and a 30-minute blast to reproduce Friday-level bursts. What would you need from us?
[06:46] Avery: we'll need your sample prompts, tokenization profile, and representative concurrency schedule. We'll provision a test harness and run token/sec and p95 traces. Also we'd like to run a streaming-only profile and a mixed profile.
[07:00] [07:20] Arjun: our networking — we prefer egress from our VPC to stay within private peering, do you have private peering options for Hosted?
[07:28] Sofia: yes we have cloud-peer and direct connect options; for strict network isolation Private is better.
[07:35] Ben: any surprises in quantization? customers earlier reported hallucination drift after 4-bit quant.
[07:42] Ravi: quantization can shift distribution; part of Redwood Optimize is to evaluate quality regressions per prompt set and surface regression alerts. We'll include that in the POC evaluation.
[07:55] [08:10] Maya: can you show an example of routing policy? e.g., prefer us-west local until backpressure > 80% then failover to standby region and fallback to quantized variant under sustained load.
[08:20] Ravi: sure — (Ravi shares screen, brief pause) — policy example: route-by-latency -> region affinity -> if queue length > 40 then route to standby region; if latency p95 > 400ms then fallback to faster quantized model; on error count > 10% send traffic to degrade route. We'll send the policy doc.
[08:40] [08:55] Leah: what's the observability we get in Redwood Console during the POC? I want token-level breakdowns,-route-level p95, and traces per token.
[09:03] Avery: Console will show token counts, per-route latency histograms, top queries causing regressions, and trace links. We can push 48h retention for the POC.
[09:14] Ben: and will we be able to run our own profiling agent to collect wall-clock at the edge?
[09:20] Sofia: yes you can instrument and combine metrics; we'll provide tracing hooks and a small sidecar for better correlating edge vs model times.
[09:29] [09:45] Maya: can Redwood do canary rollouts between model variants for A/B on quality vs cost?
[09:51] Ravi: yes, canary + weighted rollouts with automatic rollback on quality regression thresholds. We also support scheduled windows for ramping.
[09:59] [10:15] Ben: for the burst simulation — we want to run a 30-min 4x burst that increases concurrency and another with token/sec increase per stream. Your harness will simulate both?
[10:24] Avery: yes we'll simulate both modes and measure p95 and error rates, and produce a CSV with per-second tokens/sec and p95 slices.
[10:33] [10:48] Leah: curious — what about cross-region consistency for conversation state if a fallback happens mid-conversation? clients must reconcile partial tokens.
[10:57] Ravi: we recommend attaching the conversation snapshot metadata and if you need synchronous handoff we route to the same model family and replay the last N tokens; for strict linearizability you'd need a shared store. We'll detail the tradeoffs.
[11:10] [11:30] Maya: budget concerns — if we pin Dedicated to meet 15k tokens/sec, what is the rough ballpark monthly cost vs hosted pay-as-you-go?
[11:38] Avery: high-level: Dedicated run-rate might be 40–60% lower per-token at sustained throughput vs Hosted assuming steady utilization. Hosted is best for variability but higher unit cost under heavy steady load. We'll run a cost model with your utilization curve.
[11:55] Ben: do you have suggestions on batching thresholds to keep first-token p95 under 300ms?
[12:03] Ravi: aim for micro-batch window under 15ms and max batch size tuned per model; continuous batching at low queue depths preserves first-token latency. We'll provide recommended parameters for your models.
[12:16] [12:30] (background chatter)
[12:40] Maya: any gotchas with streaming and function calls? we use tool-calls to fetch DB state mid-stream.
[12:48] Sofia: tool-calls add blocking; we recommend prefetching or moving tool-call to a parallel async path; if blocking is necessary, the streaming session will buffer until the tool returns, which can spike p95. We'll discuss patterns.
[13:05] [13:22] Leah: what's the SLA for Dedicated in terms of latency — do you publish p95 latency SLAs or just uptime?
[13:30] Avery: primarily uptime SLAs but for enterprise we can commit to latency tiers as part of the contract, with observable SLOs and penalties.
[13:40] Ben: competitor question — we've been talking to AuroraServe and Anthropic about dedicated endpoints; any differentiators on routing/fallback?
[13:49] Ravi: Redwood focuses on unified routing across Hosted/Dedicated/Private and built-in KV/prefix caching; the difference is the ops experience for hybrid deployments and the Optimize toolkit for token-level economics.
[14:05] [14:20] Maya: ok sounds good. recap of what we need from you and vice versa?
[14:27] Avery: recap: Redwood will share security pack, policy examples, and test harness; we'll run a 24-hour and a 30-min burst test with your payloads. SparrowEdge will share traces, sample prompts, and expected concurrency schedule. We'll draft pilot pricing for Dedicated and a hybrid Hosted fallback plan.
[14:47] Ben: timeline? we want results within two weeks to feed next sprint planning.
[14:53] Avery: we can start bench provisioning tomorrow if we get assets today and aim to share initial results in 10 business days.
[15:02] [15:15] Action items repeated: Avery to upload harness + sample policy. Leah to share p95 traces. Ravi to draft routing policy.
[15:25] (wrap)
[15:30] Maya: thanks all, appreciate the operational detail — excited to see the harness.
[15:36] Leah: thanks — we'll send the artifacts.
[15:40] Avery: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with calendar invites for the POC scoping.

Notes on transcript quality: automated transcript had a few mis-heard acronyms (AuroraServe became "Arora-serve" in raw); speaker overlaps around minute 12 caused minor misattribution.

References shared: Redwood security pack link (will be emailed), routing policy example (will be sent), benchmark harness repo (Redwood to upload)

End of meeting.
